analysis.one_liner: Lets companies classify many workers as independent contractors instead of employees, skipping payroll taxes and benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote in the House and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a new tax-code test deciding when a worker counts as an independent contractor rather than an employee. If a company and worker meet the test—including a written contract stating the worker is not an employee—the company would not be treated as an employer for tax purposes: no payroll taxes, no withholding. Workers reclassified this way would be responsible for their own self-employment taxes and would not be employees for tax purposes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that hire workers as contractors—gig-economy platforms, staffing firms, franchisors, and other businesses with labor costs they want to keep off the payroll—would gain a statutory safe harbor. If they meet the test and file the required reports, the IRS would be sharply limited in reclassifying those workers as employees and assessing back payroll taxes. Some workers who genuinely run their own businesses would also gain certainty against audits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a statutory test under which, if the requirements are met, the worker is not treated as an employee, the payer is not treated as an employer, and compensation is not treated as employment income for tax purposes [S2][S3].

The test looks at factors like unreimbursed expenses, income fluctuation, whether the worker works exclusively for one recipient, having a place of business or bearing equipment costs, and a written contract stating the worker is not an employee and is responsible for their own taxes [S2][S3].

If a payer meets the reporting requirements, IRS reclassification of a worker as an employee generally could not take effect before a 'notice date,' and the burden of proof would shift to the Treasury Secretary once a taxpayer makes a prima facie case [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers shifted into contractor status would pay the full self-employment tax themselves and would lose employee status for tax purposes. Social Security and Medicare trust funds would lose payroll tax contributions on those wages. Taxpayers who are genuinely employees but sign the required contract could end up shouldering taxes their employers would otherwise split with them.

drawbacks.text: The written-contract test lets the parties themselves declare the relationship non-employment: a contract stating the worker 'will not be treated as an employee' is itself one of the requirements that locks in that treatment, regardless of how much control the company actually exercises over the work [S3].

Workers reclassified under the bill would be responsible for federal, state, and local taxes including self-employment taxes on their compensation, a cost employers and employees currently split [S3].
A worker who risks income fluctuations, uses a home or mobile office, or owns their equipment could be swept into contractor status under the test even if the work resembles an ordinary job [S2][S3].

The strongest good-faith case for the bill is that misclassification rules are genuinely confusing and legitimate independent contractors and small businesses face costly IRS audits; a clear safe harbor would reduce that uncertainty.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give businesses large, certain savings in payroll taxes and audit exposure. The cost falls on workers, who would lose employee tax status and bear self-employment taxes, and on Social Security and Medicare funding. Because the safe harbor can be created largely by the parties' own written contract, it risks converting ordinary jobs into contract work at the employer's option; the clarity it offers legitimate independent contractors is real but narrow by comparison.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Erik Paulsen introduced the bill on July 25, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action was taken; the committee never acted on it, and the bill died at the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept their existing employee protections and payroll tax treatment, since no company gained the safe harbor this bill would have provided. Social Security and Medicare trust funds did not lose the payroll contributions the bill would have diverted.

for.name: Erik Paulsen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a statutory worker-classification safe harbor in the tax code.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a markup or vote; no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans put their names on the bill and it never reached a vote, so the broader partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Gig-economy platforms and other businesses that hire workers as contractors
industries.note: The bill would give these firms a statutory safe harbor against IRS reclassification of their workers as employees, eliminating employer payroll taxes and reducing back-tax exposure. The savings come directly from costs currently shared with workers and payroll-tax-funded programs.
These businesses rely on classifying labor as non-employee; a written-contract safe harbor with a shifted burden of proof would make that classification far harder for the IRS to challenge.

industries.industry: Genuinely self-employed contractors and small business owners
industries.note: The bill would give legitimate independent contractors clearer rules and some protection against costly reclassification audits, the strongest honest argument for it.
